## Introduction

This page has general information about your "Final Project" for this course,
which is an **independent project** on a topic of your choice.
In it, you're expected to apply many of the things you have learned during the course.

Across four checkpoints, your Final Project is worth 50 points
(out of a total of 100 for the course).
More information about each checkpoint will be shared as the course progresses,
but here is a brief overview:

## Picking a topic

The topic and scope of the project are completely up to you.
I recommend that you take advantage of this flexibility,
so your Final Project will be as useful as possible for your own research
and/or personal development. As such:

- You may want to work with your **own data** or a publicly available dataset
  that is **similar** to data you expect to work with later.

- You are also allowed to **start** working on a larger research project in your
  Final Project, even though you many not get far enough during your Final Project
  to draw biological conclusions.

- If you're not even sure what kind of data you'll be working with in your research,
  you can simply pick something that seems of interest to you,
  and/or we could help you find something --- see below.

- Alternatively, you may prefer to focus on practicing the process that you've
  learned during this course
  (project structure, reproducibility, Slurm batch jobs, etc.)
  in your final project.
  In that case, a good choice could be to use a small,
  trivial dataset that is not necessarily relevant to your research,
  and that would be perfectly fine.

::: callout-tip
#### Contact the instructors to discuss Final Project ideas
We are happy to help you find a suitable topic and/or dataset.
More generally, we highly recommend that you contact us to discuss your
Final Project ideas before you settle on a project topic!
:::

## Graded aspects

Graded aspects of your Final Project revolve around appropriate usage of the tools
and principles we covered during the course.
To receive a high grade, your project should:

- Be **well-organized**: contained in a single parent directory with a clear and
  sensible structure of subdirectories, descriptive file and directory names,
  no files floating around with unclear purpose or source, and so on.

- Be **well-documented**, with at least one README in Markdown format in the root
  directory of your project.

- Be **version-controlled** with Git throughout: with regular, meaningful commits.
  You will need to push to GitHub at least for the proposal, draft, and final
  submission checkpoints.

- Contain **shell scripts and R scripts/Quarto documents**
  that do data processing and/or analysis.
  Beyond entering data, avoid doing manual work such as editing a data file
  in a text editor or Excel to fix column names, since this hinders reproducibility.

- Run one or more scripts as **Slurm batch jobs at OSC**
  (in general, you should do all Final Project work at OSC).

- Be easily **re-runnable** using a "protocol" in one of your Markdown files.
  After your final submission,
  we will try to rerun your project as part of the grading process!

Finally, you are allowed to use **generative AI** for your Final Project,
as long as you are still able to explain what your code does.
For example, if gen-AI comes up with some commands or constructs that we have not
see in the course,
you should do some research into those to make you understand what is being done.
You **may be asked to orally explain** your code at several points.
